## How it started

*Resident Evil* has been around for 30 years, but the survival horror series is more popular than ever. The most recent game, [*Resident Evil Requiem*](https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/883947/resident-evil-requiem-review-ps5-xbox-switch-2), has sold 8 million copies since it launched in February, already making it [the 14th best-selling game that Capcom has ever made](https://www.capcom.co.jp/ir/english/business/million.html). At the same time, [a reboot of the *Resident Evil* film series from *Weapons* director Zach Cregger](https://www.theverge.com/entertainment/996416/resident-zach-cregger-review) is on pace to become [the top-grossing movie in franchise history](https://deadline.com/2026/10/box-office-resident-evil-zach-cregger-record-1237149149/). This has had the effect of renewing interest in *Resident Evil* at large; [according to a report from *Game File*](https://www.gamefile.news/p/six-resident-evil-games-each-sold), six different titles in the game series have sold at least 3 million copies so far this year. In [an earnings report](https://www.capcom.co.jp/ir/english/data/pdf/explanation/2026/1st/explanation_2026_1st_02.pdf), Capcom called it “a virtuous cycle in which sales of both new and past titles grow together.”

*Resident Evil* isn’t alone. Rather, it’s indicative of an ongoing trend. Horror was once seen as largely a niche genre, but now, thanks to a combination of factors — including the rise of YouTube and widespread influence of indie games and viral memes — it has steadily grown into a dominant force. Horror tends to be cheaper to produce than other genres, but now it also has sales numbers that compete with the biggest blockbusters.
